title: Linked list: rewire the pointers
intro: Insert at the front, then delete from the middle, and watch which pointers move.

predict.question: To delete the middle node of a linked list, what actually changes?
options: Every later node shifts left by one
One next pointer is rewired to skip the node
The node's value is set to null
predict.reveal: The node before it gets next set to the node after it. Nothing shifts; the skipped node just becomes unreachable.

takeaway: Linked list edits are pointer rewiring: insert at the head and delete after a known node are O(1).

steps.say: A linked list is nodes chained by pointers. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. head points at the first one.
Insert 5 at the front. First make a brand new node n. It is not part of the list yet.
n.next = head: the new node points at the old first node. Nobody had to shift anywhere, just one pointer was set.
head = n: now head points at the new node. 5 is the first item. Two pointer changes and the insert is done.
Now delete 20, the middle node. We need the node BEFORE it, so p walks to 10 (head.next).

structures.name: list
structures.head: head
structures.caption: p is at 10; 20 is the target

steps.say: p.next = p.next.next: 10 now points straight at 30, hopping over 20. The list is just rewired, nothing is copied or shifted.

structures.name: unlinked
structures.caption: still points at 30, but nobody points at it

steps.say: With no pointer leading to it, node 20 is unreachable. Java's garbage collector will free it. The list is 5, 10, 30.
Compare with an array: inserting at the front of an array shifts every item. A linked list changes two pointers, however long it is.
